218.title: Pauri 33, sound: aakhan jor
218.tomorrow: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own
218.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33's repeated word jor, power, gives it a strong, hammering rhythm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 32 and the steps of the ladder. Your line was step by step. Did you take the first step of something you'd been dreading? Today, the next rung, sound first. Day two hundred eighteen.

Have you ever tried not to laugh? A quiet classroom, a serious meeting, a moment when laughing is the worst thing you could do. And it rises anyway. You bite your cheek, you stare at the floor, and your shoulders shake. Or the opposite: you want to say the right thing to a grieving friend, and nothing comes out at all. Speaking and staying quiet look like the two things a person controls best. Open mouth, close mouth. Pauri 33 opens with exactly those two, and one hard little word that keeps coming back like a hammer. Today, just listen to it.
screen: `TRYING NOT TO LAUGH.` → `THE WORDS THAT WON'T COME.` → `ONE WORD, LIKE A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 33: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Four sounds to learn. Aakhan: speaking, saying. It echoes aakheeah in yesterday's stanza, where the Name was said on a million tongues. Jor: power, force, strength. The word is still alive in everyday Punjabi; people say it when they mean push hard, put your strength into it. Chupai: in silence. You may know chup from Punjabi, as in chup kar, be quiet. Nah: not, no. So: no power to speak, no power to keep silent. Commentators read that nah across both halves of the line. Now listen to its shape. Jor lands at the end of each half: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Two short beats, then the heavy one. And the next line flips it around, so jor comes first and last: jor na mangan, den na jor. No power to ask, no power to give. The word boxes the line in. The whole stanza keeps doing this. Jor, jor, jor: ten times in eight short lines, nine of them with na or nah beside it, like someone knocking on door after door and finding every one locked. Tomorrow we'll open which doors, and whose hand holds the key. Today, feel the hammer. It's a stanza you can almost recite by the rhythm alone.
screen: `AAKHAN — SPEAKING.` · `JOR — POWER, FORCE.` · `CHUPAI NAH JOR — NOR TO BE SILENT.` · `JOR, AGAIN AND AGAIN, LIKE A HAMMER.` · then, large: `AAKHAN JOR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Say it three times, and let jor land heavy each time, like a hand on a table. Then try the next line too: jor na mangan, den na jor. After that, stop speaking, and simply stay silent. Notice that even the silence isn't quite yours: thoughts keep talking. Don't fight them. Let them knock and pass. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 33. It opens: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor, no power to speak, no power to be silent, and the word jor keeps coming back like a hammer.
Your line: aakhan jor. Today, notice one moment when words came out that you didn't plan, or didn't come when you wanted them. Just notice. Day two hundred eighteen.

219.title: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own
219.hook: no power to speak or be silent, to live or die, to beg or give; the power is in His hand (Japji 33)
219.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33 is commonly taught as a stanza against haumai, the ego that claims its own power, and its last line, no one is high or low, is often linked with Sikh teaching on equality.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 33. Your line was aakhan jor: no power to speak, none to be silent. Did words come, or not come, when you didn't plan it? Today, the whole stanza. Day two hundred nineteen.

Ask anyone who has taught a teenager to drive about the phantom brake. In the passenger seat, the teacher's right foot presses hard into the floor, again and again, where no pedal exists. A hand grips the door handle. The whole body is trying to steer a car it isn't driving. It doesn't help. It just wears them out. Plenty of people ride through life like that, gripping the outcome of the interview, the test results, the way the kids turn out. Pauri 33 walks through almost everything a person might think they control, and taps on each one.
screen: `THE PHANTOM BRAKE.` → `GRIPPING WHAT YOU DON'T DRIVE.` → `PAURI 33 TAPS ON EACH ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the list, in paraphrase. No power to speak, none to keep silent. No power to ask, none to give. No power to live, none to die. No power to hold on to kingdoms and wealth, the things that set the mind clamoring. No power over awareness, knowledge or reflection. And, one last knock on the yogis' door: no power in any technique, any jugat, to get free of the world on our own. Then comes the answer, the hand that holds what we don't: jis hath jor kar vekhai soe. The One in whose hand the power is, does it, and watches over it. And the final line: Nanak utam neech na koe. Nanak says, by themselves, no one is high and no one is low. Two things are worth noticing. First, this is not a stanza about giving up. Only a stanza ago, Japji pictured a climb step by step, and Sikh life is full of honest work and service. Sikh teachers read Pauri 33 as aimed at haumai, the ego that says I did this, all by myself. The effort is yours to make. The power behind it isn't yours to own. Second, look at where it lands. If nobody's power is their own, then nobody gets to stand above anybody else. The king with his treasury and the beggar with his bowl hold exactly the same amount of jor. It's a stanza about letting go, and it ends as a stanza about equality.
screen: `NO POWER TO SPEAK, ASK, LIVE, OR DIE.` · `NOT EVEN IN A TECHNIQUE.` · `THE POWER IS IN HIS HAND.` · `SO NO ONE IS HIGH OR LOW.` · then, large: `NOT IN MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're gripping right now: a result you're waiting for, a person you're worried about, a plan that might not work. Notice where you feel the grip in your body: jaw, shoulders, hands, stomach. Now open your hands, palms up, on your lap. You're not giving up on it. You're just taking your foot off a brake that isn't there. Breathe out, and let the shoulders drop. Stay with open hands. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 33. No power of our own to speak or be silent, to live or die, to ask or give; the power is in His hand, and so no one is high and no one is low.
Your line: not in my hands. Today, when you catch yourself pressing a phantom brake, do your part, then open your hands and let the rest go. Day two hundred nineteen.

220.title: Pauri 34, sound: raatee rutee
220.tomorrow: Pauri 34, meaning: a place for dharma
220.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 34 begins the stanzas many teachers describe as the realms, opening with a line that names night, season, lunar day and weekday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 33, and your line: not in my hands. Did you catch yourself pressing a phantom brake, and open your hands? Today, a new stanza, and it starts with time itself. Day two hundred twenty.

Picture the calendar on a kitchen wall in many Punjabi homes. It isn't just days and months. Printed in small type are the moon's phases, the full-moon days, the first day of each month when many families go to the gurdwara. Grandparents read it the way you'd read the weather: this is a good day for that, the full moon is Thursday. Time, on that wall, has layers. The night, the season, the moon, the day of the week, all stacked on top of each other. Pauri 34 opens with exactly that stack, four words long, and it sounds like a clock ticking. Today we learn to hear it.
screen: `A CALENDAR ON THE KITCHEN WALL.` → `TIME, IN LAYERS.` → `FOUR WORDS, LIKE A CLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of Pauri 34: raatee rutee thitee vaar. Four words, four kinds of time. Raatee: nights. Rutee: seasons; the word is rut, a season, the way the monsoon or the cold season comes around. Thitee: lunar days. A thit is one day of the moon's month, the days counted from new moon to full, the small print on that kitchen calendar. Vaar: the days of the week. You'll still hear it in the names of weekdays across North India: Somvaar, Mangalvaar, and so on. So in four words, Nanak lays down the whole clock: night, season, moon, week. Listen to the sound. Raatee, rutee, thitee: three words with the same shape, a short first beat and a long ee to finish, like three ticks. Then vaar, open and long, like the chime. Then the line goes on, and changes from time to things: pavan paanee aganee paataal. Air, water, fire, and the regions below. Pavan, paanee: two p's, soft as breath. Aganee: fire, a cousin of the Sanskrit agni. Paataal: the underworlds, the depths. First the clock, then the elements. Tomorrow, you'll see why Nanak sets all of this up, because in the middle of it he places something, and gives it a job. For today, just the clock and the elements, sounding.
screen: `RAATEE, RUTEE — NIGHTS, SEASONS.` · `THITEE, VAAR — MOON-DAYS, WEEKDAYS.` · `THREE TICKS AND A CHIME.` · `PAVAN PAANEE AGANEE — AIR, WATER, FIRE.` · then, large: `RAATEE RUTEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: raatee rutee thitee vaar, pavan paanee aganee paataal. Say it three times. Tick on the first three words, chime on vaar, then let the second half flow like breath. Afterward, sit quietly and notice what time it is for you, in layers. Is it day or night? What season is outside? What day of the week? Let the answers come and settle, then breathe. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 34. It opens with the whole clock in four words, nights, seasons, moon-days and weekdays, and then the elements: air, water, fire and the depths.
Your line: raatee rutee, nights and seasons. Today, step outside once and notice what season it is by the light, the air and the trees. Day two hundred twenty.

221.title: Pauri 34, meaning: a place for dharma
221.hook: nights, seasons and days, air, water and fire, and in their midst the earth set as a home for right action (Japji 34)
221.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 34 is taught as the first of the five khands, or realms, and its picture of the earth as a dharamsaal is often drawn on to describe ordinary life as the place for right action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 34. Your line was raatee rutee, nights and seasons. Did you notice the season by the light and the air? Today, what Nanak sets in the middle of all that time. Day two hundred twenty-one.

Every room you walk into tells you what it's for. A gym is for sweating. A library is for quiet. A kitchen is for feeding people. The rules come with the room, even if no one says them. Nobody jogs through a library or reads novels on the bench press. The purpose of a place shapes how you behave in it. Now zoom out. All the way out. What if someone told you what the whole earth is for? Not what it's made of or how old it is, but what it's for. Pauri 34 answers that, in one line, and gives us a new word.
screen: `A GYM, A LIBRARY, A KITCHEN.` → `EVERY PLACE HAS A PURPOSE.` → `WHAT IS THE EARTH FOR?`

segments.voice: Yesterday we heard the frame: nights, seasons, moon-days, weekdays; air, water, fire and the depths. Then comes the line the whole frame was built for: tis vich dharatee thaap rakhee dharam saal. In the middle of it all, He set the earth down as a dharamsaal, a house for dharma. Dharma here means right action, living rightly, doing what is true. In this stanza, the earth is not pictured as a waiting room or a prison. It's a place built for doing good. And the word has a life outside this stanza. Sikh tradition remembers the early places where Sikhs gathered to sing and eat together as dharamsals, before the word gurdwara became the usual one. Then the stanza fills the house. Beings of every kind and color live there, with names beyond counting. Karmee karmee hoe veechaar: each one is weighed by their own deeds. True is the One, and true the court. There the accepted ones shine, and by grace they receive the mark. Kach pakaaee othai paae: there the unripe and the ripe are sorted, like fruit. Nanak says, go there and you'll see. The next stanza will give this realm its name: Dharam Khand. Khand means a region, a realm. It's the first of five realms Japji describes: dharma, knowledge, effort, grace and truth, rising like floors of a house. And the first floor is right here, under your feet.
screen: `THE EARTH, SET AS A DHARAMSAAL.` · `DHARMA — RIGHT ACTION.` · `EACH WEIGHED BY THEIR DEEDS.` · `THE FIRST OF FIVE REALMS.` · then, large: `DHARAM KHAND.`

segments.voice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel the ground holding you. This is the dharamsaal, the house built for right action. Now choose one right thing you'll do on purpose today, something small and real: a call you owe, a mess you'll clean up, an honest answer, a kindness to someone who won't expect it. Picture yourself doing it, clearly. Then let the picture go, keep your feet on the ground, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Dharam Khand. The realm of dharma: this earth, set in the middle of time and the elements as a house for right action. The first of Japji's five realms.
Your line: the earth is for dharma. Today, do the one right thing you chose, on purpose, and notice the ground under your feet while you do it. Day two hundred twenty-one.

222.title: Pauri 35, sound: dharam khandd kaa
222.tomorrow: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
222.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 opens with a line that closes the realm of dharma and opens the realm of knowledge, then repeats kete, so many, through the rest of the stanza.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dharam Khand, the realm of right action. Your line was the earth is for dharma. Did you do your one right thing on purpose? Today, the sound of the stanza that names it. Day two hundred twenty-two.
screen: `DHARAM KHAND — THE EARTH IS FOR DHARMA.`

segments.voice: On a train, a voice comes over the speaker: this stop, Central. Next stop, Riverside. One sentence, two jobs. It closes the station you're pulling out of and names the one ahead. Nobody has to look out the window to know the trip has moved on. Pauri 35 opens with a sentence built exactly like that, a hinge between two places. And then, as soon as the next place comes into view, one small word starts repeating, over and over, as if the speaker keeps turning around and finding more. Today, the hinge and the word.
screen: `THIS STOP.` → `NEXT STOP.` → `A HINGE BETWEEN TWO PLACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the hinge: dharam khandd kaa eho dharam, giaan khandd kaa aakhahu karam. Take the first half. Dharam khandd: the realm of dharma, yesterday's word, sung with a strong double d at the end, khandd. Kaa: of. Eho: this, this very. Dharam: dharma. So: this is the dharma of the realm of dharma. That's this stop, closing behind us. Everything Pauri 34 said, the earth as a house for right action, each weighed by their deeds, that's the way of that realm. Now the second half. Giaan khandd: the realm of knowledge. You met giaan in Pauri 29, wisdom as the meal. Kaa: of. Aakhahu: tell, speak of it; you can hear aakhan from Pauri 33 in it. Karam: here, the doings, the workings. So: now tell of the workings of the realm of knowledge. That's the next stop. Listen to how the two halves rhyme on their last words: dharam, karam. Then comes the word that repeats: kete. It means how many, so many. Kete pavan paanee vaisantar, so many winds, waters and fires. Kete, kete, kete, line after line, as if the speaker keeps turning and finding more. By the end of the stanza you've heard kete more than a dozen times. Tomorrow we'll see what's being counted. Today, hear the hinge swing, and hear kete begin.
screen: `DHARAM KHANDD KAA EHO DHARAM.` · `GIAAN KHANDD KAA AAKHAHU KARAM.` · `DHARAM, KARAM — THE HINGE RHYMES.` · `KETE — SO MANY, SO MANY.` · then, large: `DHARAM KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: dharam khandd kaa eho dharam, giaan khandd kaa aakhahu karam. Say it three times. Feel the first half close, and the second half open. Then sit, and imagine the pause at a station: the doors open, one stop behind you, the next one ahead. Behind you, everything you already know. Ahead, something larger. Don't move yet. Just stay in the pause and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 35. It opens with a hinge: this is the way of the realm of dharma; now tell of the realm of knowledge. And then the word kete, so many, begins.

Your line: dharam khandd. Today, when you finish one task and before you start the next, take one breath in between, and notice what you're leaving and what you're starting. Day two hundred twenty-two.

223.title: Pauri 35, meaning: the realm of knowledge
223.hook: beyond duty is the realm of knowledge: winds, waters, suns and worlds without number (Japji 35)
223.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 35 is taught as the realm of knowledge, the second of the five khands, and its long list of kete, so many, is often read as the ego opening up before the vastness of creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 35, the hinge between two realms. Your line was dharam khandd. Did you pause in a doorway? Today, we walk through into the realm of knowledge. Day two hundred twenty-three.

Astronomers once pointed a space telescope at a tiny patch of sky that looked completely empty. Dark. Nothing there. They left the camera open a long time, collecting whatever faint light trickled in. When the picture came back, that empty patch was full of galaxies, each one a city of stars. A picture like that can make the floor drop away. The universe is bigger than anyone can hold in mind. Japji has a name for the place where that dizziness lives, and it got there with no telescope at all. It calls it the realm of knowledge.
screen: `AN EMPTY PATCH OF SKY.` → `FULL OF GALAXIES.` → `THE FLOOR DROPS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday the hinge swung: this is the way of the realm of dharma; now tell of the realm of knowledge. Gian Khand. In the first realm, you learn to live rightly on this earth. In the second, your eyes open to how big everything actually is. And Nanak shows you by counting, and failing to finish. Kete, so many. So many winds, waters and fires. So many lands where deeds are done, so many great mountains. So many moons, so many suns, so many worlds and lands. He reaches for figures his listeners honored, the creator Brahma, Krishna, Shiva, the great teachers and sages, and says: there are so many of them too. The point isn't to make anyone small. It's to show how big the whole is. Then the list turns to us: so many ways that life begins, so many languages, so many kings, so many kinds of awareness, so many who serve. And the stanza ends: Nanak ant na ant. There is no end to its end. Notice what knowledge means here. It's not a pile of facts. It's the moment the facts become too many to hold, and the heart goes quiet in wonder. Some Sikh teachers say this realm breaks the small self open. You can't stay the center of the world once you've seen how many worlds there are. In the stanza, that isn't a loss. It's where wonder starts.
screen: `GIAN KHAND — THE REALM OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `KETE — SO MANY SUNS, SO MANY WORLDS.` · `NANAK ANT NA ANT — NO END TO ITS END.` · `KNOWING, UNTIL WONDER TAKES OVER.` · then, large: `SO MANY WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes. Picture the room you're in, then the building, then your town from above. Keep rising: the country, the whole earth turning, the sun, the other planets, the Milky Way, and then galaxy after galaxy, so many. Don't try to hold it all. Let it be too big. When you feel small, notice whether it feels like loss, or like relief. Then come back to your breath, one breath in one body. The bell holds the time.
Gian Khand. The realm of knowledge, where your eyes open to so many winds, suns and worlds that the counting never ends. The second of Japji's five realms.
Your line: so many worlds. Today, learn one new thing about the universe, one fact about stars or planets or deep time, and let it make you small in a good way. Day two hundred twenty-three.

224.title: Pauri 36, sound: giaan khandd
224.tomorrow: Pauri 36, meaning: the realm of effort
224.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 36 opens with giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd, still in the realm of knowledge, before the stanza turns to the realm of effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gian Khand, the realm of knowledge. Your line was so many worlds. Did you learn one new thing about the universe? Today, the end of a week, and the start of the last climb. Day two hundred twenty-four.

Look back down the ladder at this week. Aakhan jor: no power to speak, none to be silent, and the power not in my hands. Raatee rutee: nights and seasons, the whole clock. Then the earth set down as a house for right action: the earth is for dharma. Dharam khandd, the hinge. And yesterday, so many worlds. Six rungs. Now the Japji enters its last stretch: three more stanzas and a final salok. Now a fire. Not a candle: a bonfire at night, so bright the faces around it glow and the dark beyond goes darker. Nobody near it looks anywhere else. Pauri 36 begins with a line that burns like that.
screen: `A WEEK: NOT IN MY HANDS, THE CLOCK, DHARMA.` → `A BONFIRE AT NIGHT.` → `A LINE THAT BURNS.`

segments.voice: Here is how Pauri 36 opens: giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd. Giaan khandd: the realm of knowledge, the one we walked into yesterday. Meh: in. Giaan: knowledge. Parchandd: blazing, fierce, like a fire at full strength or the sun at noon. In the realm of knowledge, knowledge blazes. Listen to how the line doubles its word. Giaan, then giaan again, the second one on fire. It's as if Nanak is standing inside the realm and the word itself catches light. Then the next line: tithai naad binod kodd anand. Tithai: there. Naad: the sound, the note, the same word from Pauri 29, sounding in every heart. Binod: play, delight. Kodd: ten million, a crore, a number too big to picture. Anand: joy, bliss. There, music, play, and joy by the millions. Now hear the rhyme that holds the two lines together: parchandd, anand. The fire, then the joy. The first line is bright and hard, with that strong dd at the end. The second is soft and wide, and ends on an open breath. Tomorrow the stanza turns to a new realm with a new word, and we'll open its meaning. Today, just stand in the blaze and let it sound. And notice what Nanak puts inside a realm of knowledge. Not lecture halls. Music, play and joy.
screen: `GIAAN KHANDD MEH — IN THE REALM OF KNOWING.` · `GIAAN PARCHANDD — KNOWLEDGE BLAZES.` · `NAAD, BINOD — MUSIC AND PLAY.` · `KODD ANAND — JOY BY THE MILLIONS.` · then, large: `GIAAN KHANDD.`

segments.voice: Say the first two lines aloud, slowly: giaan khandd meh giaan parchandd, tithai naad binod kodd anand. Say them three times. Let the first line be bright and firm, and the second soft and wide, ending on an open breath. Then sit quietly and imagine warm light in the center of your chest, steady, like a flame out of the wind. Let it glow as you breathe. No need to think about anything. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 36. It opens in the realm of knowledge, where knowledge blazes, and there is music, play and joy by the millions.
Your line: giaan khandd, the realm of knowledge. Today, when you understand something new, let it be a joy and not just a fact: smile at it. Day two hundred twenty-four.
